title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively a Company Spent on AI in H1, the Sooner It Gets Discounted
dek: Capital markets can only rise if new money keeps buying in. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that were most aggressive on AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain, offering a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.
who: For investors watching both US AI stocks and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for private-market practitioners judging where and when hot money will flow in 2025.
skip: The discussion of individual Hong Kong IPO cases can be skipped; the main thread picks up at 8:11 with Nvidia's liquidity experiment.

points.h: A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
points.body: Do not take the low first-day break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of a strengthening market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level that a market-based mechanism would produce. That means the main participants in these IPOs are short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of new listings has shrunk and an IPO-related fund blew up, yet the two most recent listings still broke issue price, showing that temporary supply-side controls have not solved the underlying problem: Hong Kong also faces peak liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
points.body: Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were released in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capex in the first half, especially those that burned through free cash flow, was discounted—even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the entire supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before prices rose, and inventory still propping up gross margins. By Q3, as inventory runs out and price increases feed through, the negative factors will all show up together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out rent-to-own deals to help customers finance purchases, pulling future revenue forward into current sales. Nvidia is now pushing rent-to-own as well. In its financials, free cash flow halved quarter-on-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—this is suspected to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure that rent-to-own brings. So Nvidia may have reached the stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Private market money comes from bullets loaded three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in the timing of fund fundraising. The money that will be deployed into AI and robotics in H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. They barely invested in 2023-2025, until they saw state capital placing bets during a period when no one dared to invest and earning the most—stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large language models, and two big chip companies stimulated market-based capital. The mindset is: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term incremental wave, but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: The new property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key to recent real estate policy is not bailing out developers, but pulling households out of the old financing loop. In the past, buying a pre-sale home meant the household played the role of financier in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive the home later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers get completed homes and only play the consumer role, with risk reset back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom in order to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side and avoid panic from dismantling the chain during a downturn. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining industry consolidations followed similar paths.

points.h: A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
points.body: A slow bull does not rely on slogans; it relies on layering market chips by duration. At the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long money that rarely trades. Above that are mutual funds and index funds, playing a quasi-stabilizing role. Above that, Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjust the index. At the top are retail investors, private funds and active managers. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in term, yield and liquidity, effectively ensuring long money for long investments, medium money for medium investments, and short money for short investments—no using ordinary people's short-term money to invest in ten-year illiquid assets.

points.h: Crises get bigger with each rescue, and bubbles at least one and a half times
points.body: After the US dollar decoupled from gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to intervening in crises directly by printing money, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been unwound during a rate-hiking cycle, but political interference interrupted it, and then the pandemic hit in 2020, so a larger wave of easing was layered on top of a bubble that had not yet dissipated—today we have accumulated at least one and a half bubbles. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis emerges, and the endogenous result is that inflation, rising financial assets and wealth inequality all intensify together. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face long-term stagflation in some form.

quotes.text: The reason I say it feels a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a bit of a peak liquidity problem.
In the capital markets, whoever spends aggressively is seen as impressive, and then when half-year reports come out, it becomes whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where it needs rent-to-own to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone looks and says, if you can pull off this story like that, then I can certainly pull off this story like that too—psychologically it's roughly like that.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently both slow and bullish; on the basis of a slow bull, you first have to build a chip structure.
When the bubble piled up last time had not yet dissipated, a bigger one was added on top—and it was added without hesitation.
